# Combining vector layers {#sec-e04}

> **Date of practical:** 23rd and 30th October 2026

Creating spatial and thematic subsets of vector layers is essential GIS practice. It is through the manipulation and combination of spatial datasets that new information is generated - such as where to site a wind farm.

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives

To clip small subsets from large vector datasets, create dissolved buffers around line and polygon layers, select subsets by attribute, and combine layers necessary for making Map 2.
:::

## Investigating your map tile

(@) Launch QGIS and create a new project

(@) From the `UK_Boundaries` folder, add the `Wales_border.gpkg` layer to your project

(@) From the `Wales_map_tiles` folder, add your [assigned OS map tile](https://canvas.swansea.ac.uk/courses/69491/pages/key-information-2?module_item_id=4214484){target='_blank'} to your project. This layer is where your wind farm project will focus

(@) Calculate the area of your map tile in square kilometres. Need reminding of how to do this? See @sec-measuring

(@) Calculate the perimeter of your map tile in kilometres

(@) This time, allow QGIS to do the heavy lifting by calculating area and perimeter for you using the field calculator. Because all master layers on OneDrive cannot be edited, you will first need to save a copy of the map tile to your own OneDrive account. Remember how to export a layer? If not, see @sec-export

## Using the field calculator {#sec-fieldcalc}

(@) The field calculator is a powerful tool that lets you create new attribute fields or update existing ones using fast mathematical, geometric, and conditional expressions. Calculate the area of your tile:

    i. Open the attribute table for your map tile copy. This layer has one polygon, so there's only one row in the table
    ii. Click the `Open field calculator` icon (![](figs/FieldCalculator.png){width=3%})
    iii. In `Output field name` type `Area`
    iv. Set `Output field type` as `Decimal number (real)`
    v. In the middle panel, expand the `Geometry` drop-down menu
    vi. Double-click `$area`
    vii. Click `OK`
    viii. Click the `Save edits` icon (![](figs/SaveEdits.png){width=3%} )to save the changes to the attribute table
    ix. Click the `Toggle editing mode` icon (![](figs/ToggleEditingMode.png){width=3%}) to turn off editing mode

(@) Calculate the `$perimeter` of your map tile as well. Now these values have been saved in the attribute table, what units are these in? Note that the values are slightly different from what you should have expected. This is because the curvature of the Earth introduces a small distortion between real and mapped areas

(@) From everything you learnt in @sec-e03, calculate the number of people living within your polygon at the 2021 Census

(@) Using the area measurement you calculated above, compute population density for your tile. This might be a useful piece of information to present in a caption!

## Clipping layers {#sec-clip}

(@) Add all the layers in the `Wales_protected_areas` folder to your project

(@) Explore these layers and their attributes. Is it obvious what is meant by 'protected areas'? Find more information about these datasets [here](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protected_areas_of_Wales){target='_blank'}.

(@) Save your project!

(@) Clip each protected area layer so they appear within your map tile:

    i. Click `Vector` → `Geoprocessing Tools` → `Clip...`
    ii. Set `Input layer` to one of the protected areas layers (e.g. `NRW_AONB`)
    iii. Set `Overlay layer` to your map tile
    iv. Click `Run` → `Close`
    
::: {.callout-warning}
## Temporary scratch layers

You'll now see a new layer called `Clipped` with a memory chip icon (![](figs/TempScratchLayer.png){width=3%}) next to it. This means the layer is temporary. If you close QGIS now, you will lose temporary layers. The value and vulnerabilities of temporary layers came up in the last exercise.
:::

(@) Right-click the `Clipped` layer → click `Rename Layer`

(@) Rename the layer something more intuitive (e.g. `NRW_AONB_Clipped`). It is important to rename temporary layers as you go, otherwise you'll inevitably get confused over which layers represent what 

(@) Clip the remaining protected area datasets to your map tile. You only need to clip those layers that actually have features in your area, so inspect the layers first to find out if this is the case

## Merging layers {#sec-merge}

(@) Merge the clipped layer to create a single 'protected area' layer:

    i. Click `Vector` → `Data Management Tools` → `Merge Vector Layers...`
    ii. Under `Input layers`, click the `Browse` icon (![](figs/Browse.png){width=3%}) and check all the clipped layers
    iii. Click `OK`
    iv. Set `Destination CRS` to `EPSG:27700`
    v. Click `Run` → `Close`

## Dissolving layers {#sec-dissolve}

(@) Combining polygons often leaves behind boundaries within the output which no longer represent the new polygon edge. These may even complicate further processing steps. It is good practice to remove these internal boundaries using the `Dissolve` tool. Dissolve internal boundaries of the merged layer:

    i. Click `Vector` → `Geoprocessing Tools` → `Dissolve...`
    ii. Set `Input layer` to your merged layer
    iii. Click `Run` → `Close`

(@) Now you have the final product derived from a series of processing steps, export the layer (forgotten how? see @sec-export)

(@) Use the field calculator to find total protected area. Calculate percentage of your tile. This might be a useful piece of information to present in a caption!

(@) Have you been saving your project?

::: {.callout-tip}
## Efficient filing

This is a good time to remind you to be careful and tidy about where to save GIS output. You will be generating many files for this project, and a hierarchical folder structure and carefully named layers is highly recommended. Be methodical in how you
name layers and where you put them. You will need to find and use them later on.
:::

## Buffering layers

(@) Check the [Map 2 constraints](https://canvas.swansea.ac.uk/courses/69491/assignments/674932){target='_blank'} that must be followed, including that windfarm should not be placed within specified distances of key geographic features

(@) From the `British_Isles_geofabrik/wales` folder, add the `gis_osm_waterways_free_1.gpkg`, `gis_osm_water_a_free_1.gpkg`, `gis_osm_railways_free_1.gpkg`, and `gis_osm_roads_free_1.gpkg` constraint layers to your project

(@) Add the `Wales_operational_windfarms.gpkg` constraint layer to your project

(@) Explore these constraint layers' attributes

(@) Clip each of these constraint layers to your tile (though there may be none in your map tile) and name them sensibly

(@) Buffers are a useful way to mark out areas that fall within the constraint distances. Create buffers around the newly added features:

    i. Click `Vector` → `Geoprocessing Tools` → `Buffer...`
    ii. Set `Input layer` to one of the constraint layers (e.g. `gis_osm_roads_free_1`)
    iii. Set `Distance` to `150` (see [Map 2 constraints](https://canvas.swansea.ac.uk/courses/69491/assignments/674932){target='_blank'})
    iv. Check `Dissolve result`
    v. Click `Run` → `Close`

(@) Create buffers around all transport link, water body, and existing windfarm layers

## Exporting specific elements from a layer {#sec-selexpress}

(@) From the `British_Isles_geofabrik/wales` folder, add the `gis_osm_landuse_a_free_1.gpkg` layer to your project

(@) Clip the layer to your map tile

(@) Select subsets of this data using an expression:

    i. Open the layer's attribute table
    ii. Click `Select features using an expression` (![](figs/SelectByExpression.png){width=3%})
    iii. Expand `Fields and Values`
    vi. Click `fclass` → `All Unique`. All unique categories in the `fclass` layer (i.e. all the unique land use classes) are now listed
    v. Under `Expression`, type `"fclass" = 'residential'`. You can also double-click on the fields, values, and symbols (e.g. ![](figs/Equals2.png){width=3%}) to build the expression
    vi. Click `Select Features` → `Close`

(@) Export the selected polygons (remember to use the `Save Selected Features As...` option). Name and store methodically

(@) Repeat for all other relevant land use classes (again, refer to [Map 2 constraints and considerations](https://canvas.swansea.ac.uk/courses/69491/assignments/674932){target='_blank'})

## Taking stock of planning constraints

(@) By this point you should have a set of data layers which together represent those parts of your map tile unsuitable for windfarm development because of their position within, or proximity to, man-made or natural features of the landscape. Consider how best to present these on a map as part of your Project. Remember to think about the purpose and audience, and the need to justify your thinking. Would clipping your buffers remove trailing bits beyond your map tile? In the same way you created a 'protected areas' layer from AONB, NP, SSSI, etc., can you do the same for transport links and water bodies? Experimentation is encouraged!

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning outcomes

By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

1. Use the field calculator to derive geometric attributes (area, perimeter) and compute values such as population density for a map tile.
2. Clip features from large vector datasets to a defined area of interest, retaining only the data relevant to the analysis.
3. Combine multiple clipped layers into a single dataset by merging and dissolving internal boundaries to produce clean output.
4. Create dissolved buffers around line and polygon features to represent zones of constraint or proximity.
5. Select features by attribute using expressions, and organise the resulting layers methodically within a well-structured file system.
:::
